common_name: Sir Walter St. Augustinegrass (Australian-Bred Soft-Leaf Buffalo Grass)

planting.note: Lay sod or set plugs on 12-inch centers once soil is warm and irrigate daily for the first two to three weeks until runners knit together.

directions: Bred in Australia and marketed there as a buffalo grass, Sir Walter carries broader, soft blue-green blades and a dense, self-repairing runner habit that fills in foot traffic wear faster than many older St. Augustine selections. It holds decent color into cooler months and tolerates moderate shade under high tree canopies, though it still wants at least four to five hours of direct or bright filtered light to stay dense. Mow at 3 to 4 inches with a sharp blade to avoid shredding the wide leaf, and watch for chinch bugs and gray leaf spot, the same pressures that affect other St. Augustine cultivars in humid Gulf Coast summers. Water deeply and infrequently once established, since shallow frequent irrigation encourages a weak root system and disease.
sources: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries — Turf Variety Guide

common_name: Tiflawn Bermudagrass (Original Coarse-Bladed Tifton Sports-Turf Hybrid)

planting.note: Establish only from sprigs, plugs, or sod once soil has warmed, since this sterile hybrid produces no viable seed.

directions: Released in 1952 from the Tifton, Georgia breeding program, Tiflawn was the first controlled hybrid between common and African bermudagrass and later became the seed parent used to develop the finer-textured Tifgreen and Tifway lines. It is coarser and more vigorous than its descendants, which makes it too rough for putting greens but well suited to hard-wearing applications like ballfields, playgrounds, and rough utility turf that need fast lateral recovery from traffic damage. It spreads aggressively by both stolons and rhizomes, tolerates close mowing down to about an inch, and holds up to heat and drought better than common bermuda seed types. Because it no longer matches modern fine-textured lawn expectations, it is mostly grown today for historical interest and heavy-use sports surfaces rather than residential lawns.
sources: University of Georgia — History of Bermudagrass Breeding Research in Tifton

common_name: Midlawn Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Kansas-Bred Hybrid Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Plant sprigs or sod after the last frost; Midlawn was bred for the transition zone and tolerates a shorter warm season than Gulf Coast hybrids.

directions: Selected through open pollination at the Kansas State University polycross nursery in Fort Hays, Midlawn was released for its exceptional cold hardiness, surviving temperatures near minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit that kill most hybrid bermudagrasses. It rated highest for winter survival among more than two dozen cultivars in transition-zone trials, making it a fit for the northern edge of bermuda's range rather than deep South lawns. It forms a dense, drought-resistant sod with medium-fine texture and recovers quickly from winter injury once temperatures rise in spring. Like other hybrid bermudas it needs full sun and regular mowing to stay dense, and it should be renovated by dethatching or verticutting in late spring to remove winter-killed tissue.
sources: Kansas State University Research Foundation — Midlawn Bermudagrass Plant Patent

planting.note: Establish vegetatively from sprigs or sod; this triploid hybrid is sterile and produces no viable seed.

directions: Released cooperatively by Kansas State and Oklahoma State University breeders, Midfield is a triploid hybrid selected primarily for superior cold hardiness and turf quality on athletic fields near the northern limit of bermudagrass adaptation. Its sterility prevents unwanted seed production and off-type volunteers, a benefit for sports fields where playing surface uniformity matters. It produces a fine-to-medium-textured, dense sod that recovers well from wear damage during the growing season, though it goes dormant and turns brown earlier in fall than Gulf Coast cultivars. Overseeding with a cool-season grass or applying a pigment can maintain color through the dormant months in its transition-zone range.
sources: Kansas State University Research Foundation — Midfield Bermudagrass Plant Patent

common_name: Midway Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy Transition-Zone Hybrid Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Set sprigs or sod after the last frost; developed for transition-zone winters, it establishes well even where the warm season is short.

directions: Developed at Kansas State University during the 1960s and released in 1991 alongside Midlawn, Midway was bred specifically for cold hardiness in transition-zone lawns and sports turf where standard hybrid bermudas suffer frequent winterkill. It produces a medium-textured, moderately dense sod with good drought tolerance once established and recovers reliably from winter dieback compared with Gulf Coast-adapted cultivars grown too far north. It requires full sun and well-drained soil, and because it is less refined in texture than newer dwarf hybrids, it is best suited to general lawns and utility turf rather than close-mown ornamental applications. Regular spring dethatching helps remove winter-damaged tissue and speeds green-up.

common_name: Savannah Bermudagrass (Improved Fine-Textured Seeded Lawn Grass)

planting.note: Broadcast hulled seed at 1-2 lbs per 1,000 square feet once soil temperatures are reliably above 65 degrees F and keep the seedbed evenly moist until germination.

directions: Savannah is a seeded common-type bermudagrass bred for a darker green color, finer leaf texture, and deeper root system than older, unimproved common bermuda seed lots, placing it a step closer to hybrid-quality turf while still being economical to establish from seed. It was evaluated in the National Bermudagrass Test and rated among the better-performing seeded selections for overall turf quality in regional trials. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but, like all bermudagrass, thins quickly under shade and needs a minimum of six hours of direct sun daily. Mow regularly at 1 to 2 inches during the growing season and avoid overwatering, which promotes thatch and weakens drought tolerance.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Seeded Turf-Type Bermudagrasses

common_name: CitraZoy Zoysiagrass (University of Florida Fine-Textured Winter-Color Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs after the last frost, watering daily for the first two to three weeks until it roots in.

directions: Released by the University of Florida in 2019, CitraZoy is a fine-bladed zoysia selected for retaining green winter color longer than most other zoysiagrasses, a trait that makes it stand out in Florida trial plots through the cooler months. Its shade tolerance falls between typical Zoysia japonica and Zoysia matrella cultivars, giving it more flexibility than Empire or Meyer under partial tree canopy while still forming a dense, wear-tolerant lawn in full sun. It has shown strong resistance to large patch disease in university trials, though it remains susceptible to leaf spot in humid conditions, so avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering late in the day. Mow at 1 to 2 inches with a sharp reel or rotary blade to keep the fine texture from fraying.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Zoysiagrass for Florida Lawns

common_name: Pristine Flora Zoysiagrass (University of Florida Fine-Bladed Manilagrass Selection)

planting.note: Establish from sod or plugs once soil is warm; this fine-textured manilagrass knits together slowly, so keep newly planted areas consistently moist.

directions: Originally released by the University of Florida in 2004 under the designation BA-305, this Zoysia matrella selection produces a dense, fine-bladed, low-growing turf comparable to Zeon and Diamond in overall quality. In university insect trials it showed reduced feeding damage and lower billbug larval infestations compared with several other zoysia cultivars, suggesting somewhat better resilience against this common zoysia pest. It tolerates close mowing and full sun exposure well, making it suitable for higher-end residential lawns, but it is slower to establish and repair itself than coarser Zoysia japonica types. Scout regularly for billbugs and mole crickets and avoid excess nitrogen, which increases thatch buildup in fine-textured zoysias.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Zoysiagrass for Florida Lawns
Journal of Economic Entomology — Zoysiagrass Genotype Responses to Billbugs

planting.note: Establish only from sod or plugs after soil has warmed; this fine-bladed manilagrass spreads slowly and benefits from tight plug spacing for faster fill-in.

directions: Released in 2008, Rollmaster is a Zoysia matrella cultivar bred for the narrow, wiry, pointed leaf blades typical of manilagrass, giving it a dense, carpet-like texture favored on golf course tees, fairways, and high-end lawns. It tolerates very low mowing heights without losing density, and once established it needs comparatively little fertilizer or supplemental water to stay attractive. Like other fine zoysias it establishes slowly from plugs or sod, so weed control during the first growing season is important while the turf knits together. Full sun produces the tightest, most uniform stand, though it can tolerate light shade with some thinning.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Zoysiagrass for Florida Lawns

planting.note: Sow a light rate of hulled seed into a weed-free bed once soil is reliably warm; can also be established from sod or plugs.

directions: Patented as a distinct centipedegrass selection, SS-0705 is characterized by uniformly green stolons and foliage, short narrow leaf blades, and notably good fall color retention and cold hardiness compared with older seed-propagated centipede lots. It grows at a medium rate with low aggressiveness, a trait breeders selected for because it reduces thatch buildup and mowing frequency, fitting the low-input reputation centipedegrass is known for. Like all centipedegrass it prefers acidic, sandy soils and performs poorly with heavy nitrogen or lime applications, which induce iron chlorosis and winter injury. Mow high, at 2 to 3 inches, and irrigate only during extended dry spells once the stand is established.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP31177 — Eremochloa ophiuroides 'SS-0705'

common_name: Tift TC458 Centipedegrass (Tifton-Bred Seed-Propagated Turf Selection)

planting.note: Sow hulled seed into a weed-free bed once soil is reliably warm, or establish from sprigs or sod.

directions: Developed through the Tifton, Georgia turfgrass breeding program that produced TifBlair, Tift TC458 is a diploid centipedegrass that can be propagated by seed or vegetatively by sprigs or sod, giving installers flexibility not available with every centipede release. It forms the coarse, apple-green, slow-growing turf typical of the species, requiring infrequent mowing and minimal fertility once established. As with other centipedegrasses, it performs best on acidic, well-drained sandy soils and should never receive lime or heavy nitrogen, both of which trigger iron chlorosis and winter dieback. Its low input needs make it well suited to homeowners who want a low-maintenance lawn and are willing to accept a coarser texture and slower recovery from wear than hybrid bermudagrass or zoysia.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP35758 — Centipedegrass 'Tift TC458'

common_name: Bluebank Kentucky Bluegrass (Super Elite Traffic-Tolerant Sports Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Best seeded in late summer to early fall, or early spring in colder regions; keep the seedbed evenly moist through the slow bluegrass germination period.

directions: Bluebank is a Super Elite-rated Kentucky bluegrass bred for professional sports turf, combining strong traffic tolerance and rhizome-driven self-repair with dark green color, medium-fine texture, and good density in NTEP-style trials. Its aggressive rhizome spread allows it to recover from divot damage and heavy wear faster than many older bluegrass cultivars, a key reason it is favored for stadium and tournament golf course use. It shows solid resistance to common bluegrass diseases when mowed and fertilized appropriately, but like all Kentucky bluegrass it performs best in full sun with regular irrigation and struggles in shade or extended summer heat. It is not adapted to Gulf Coast or other warm-humid climates and is intended for cool-season and transition-zone lawns and athletic fields.
sources: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program (NTEP) — Kentucky Bluegrass Test
